sm: The hosts open with the wave of outages and shutdowns that hit the country ahead of Thanksgiving, including the FAA shutdown, Microsoft Outlook problems, airline glitches, a PlayStation outage and a cyber attack that Chase admitted to. Tim Rice argues it is not as bad as people think, suggesting some events may be warning shots from a regime like Iran or downstream effects of foiled attacks, while social contagion makes every failure a headline. Mary Margaret Olohan and Tim cite Karoline Leavitt's call for more transparency, saying that repeating that there is no evidence of malicious activity is not comforting.

The conversation turns to the White House's communications problem, with staff departures and no press secretary, and a hearing and press conference involving Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy. Some on the panel believe Iran is probing American systems and letting the country know its capabilities. They note that panic began before the shutdowns, partly from online chatter about a global shutdown and from confusion over the Pentagon's Project Fortress, which put military bases on their own power grids. They say future administrations will have to learn to handle viral outrage and technology meltdowns.

The panel discusses Mullin's defensive hearing on Capitol Hill, a government plane trip to the Texas and LSU game, and the larger problem of Senate confirmations in a divided Congress. They argue that any new cabinet nominee would need Democratic votes, so acting officials may fill posts for two years, which is especially hard at Homeland Security. They say personal affection from the president is the best sign of job security. They then turn to the investigative playbook Democrats are expected to follow once they hold power, which one speaker describes as aimed at vengeance, and they warn that voters may tire of hearings, much as they tired of Hillary Clinton's emails.

The hosts debate whether Democratic investigations will help or hurt them. One view is that Trump fatigue is the biggest threat to Republicans, and that Democrats could drive the news cycle every day. Others argue that targeting young staffers will look petty, and that Republicans can point to real corruption and to past overreaches like the Russia investigation and January 6th hearings. They also discuss Democrats winning on affordability without having solved it, and how that argument can be turned against them.

Brent Cher describes his sit-down with Senate Majority Leader John Thune, who is surprisingly optimistic about working with moderate Democrats. The panel considers why Republicans may feel freer in the minority, including less pressure from Trump posts on Truth Social. They discuss a coming funding fight in December and Trump's lingering influence through endorsements, with an Arkansas example where his attacks had little effect. Tim and others question how much Trump will push specific legislation, citing the SAVE Act.

The panel talks about Trump's post-election remark that he could work with Democrats, and the areas where a deal might happen, including AI, data centers and China, and cyber attacks. They disagree about whether this is good news. One host is skeptical that Congress can do anything, and says he would prefer nothing to a compromise on immigration that every conservative hates. Others note Trump is not a party loyalist on some economic issues, such as drug price controls, and discuss AI guardrails and the risk of Chuck Schumer influencing him.

They then look at Democrats in the House and Senate, wondering whether they will learn the wrong lessons from the midterms and force new shutdown fights, including over the Iran war. They point out a possible split between House and Senate Democrats and a coming funding deadline, and say prediction markets give a shutdown notable odds. Several argue nobody wants a shutdown and that Democrats may be risk averse until they take power. The show ends with a lighthearted round on favorite Thanksgiving dishes, with stuffing, mashed potatoes and stuffed mushrooms mentioned, and a farewell until next week.
sg: Bipartisan deals and the shutdown fight
